text: An all-female SWAT team from China beat an all-male police team from the US, and video of the matchup is going viral. During the UAE SWAT Challenge in Dubai, China's Sichuan Police all-female squad went head-to-head against the Orlando Police Department in the Officer Rescue event. The course required parrying a massive 120kg tyre across the finish line without rolling, dragging or throwing it. While the Orlando team relied on raw muscle power, the Sichuan squad executed flawless, synchronised leverage, lifting as a single unit without a single fumble. Work smarter. The Chinese officers finished the event in 3 minutes flat, beating Orlando PD by 16 seconds. So why is this video suddenly blowing up everywhere? Is it because we don't pay enough attention to women in high-level competition? Or are we just shocked when pure technique beats brute force? Are you guys tired of huge news outlets with millions of followers fueling gender war propaganda and manipulating the information they present? I hope not! Because I've got another great example for you today. This is News.com.au, an Australian news outlet that describes itself as Australia's number one news site, and they published a video about a Chinese all-female SWAT team beating an American all-male SWAT team in a competition. Then they followed it up by claiming that history shows this is no anomaly, and that women have been outplaying men for over a century. And the video went viral. When I checked, it had around 2.4 million views, close to 400,000 likes and almost 5,500 comments, many of them praising how great the women are, how they are better than men, and also how basically men suck. And hey, there's absolutely nothing wrong with praising women. Women are great at many things, that goes without question. But I'm sorry ladies, I have to say this. This huge news outlet just shamelessly manipulated you. So what actually happened? Well, between February 7th and 11th, 2026, Dubai hosted the 7th UAE SWAT Challenge. This is an international competition for specialized police and tactical units organized by Dubai Police. And this year, it brought together 109 teams from 48 countries. The competition consisted of five different challenges held over five days. This included shooting exercises, hostage and officer rescue scenarios, climbing towers, and navigating obstacle courses. The teams were evaluated based on their performance, including completion times and penalties for mistakes. And importantly, this wasn't a competition between Chinese women and American men. There were teams from dozens of countries, including eight all-female teams and two mixed-gender teams competing in the same overall tournament. Now, let's go back to the video. The footage they showed comes from day three, which was the officer rescue challenge. And yes, the Chinese women's team and Orlando Police Department both participated in this event. But here's something rather important that the news outlet didn't explain. These two teams were not actually racing against each other. The news report tells you that they went head-to-head and presents their performances side-by-side, as if this were some kind of direct contest between the Chinese women and the American men. But that's not how the competition worked. Each team performed its own run separately, and the results were compared afterwards. In fact, the organizers uploaded the entire day three competition to their official YouTube channel. And you can literally watch the teams completing the course one after another. So the side-by-side video you're watching is an edited comparison of two separate performances, not an actual head-to-head race. Now, you might say, well, who cares? If the Chinese women completed the course faster, doesn't that still mean they beat the American men? And the answer is yes, they absolutely did. The Chinese women's team, officially called China Police Team F, completed the challenge in just over three minutes, while Orlando Police Department took approximately three minutes and 16 seconds. And actually, Orlando received an additional 10-second penalty, meaning that the difference in their official results was about 26 seconds, rather than the 16 seconds mentioned in the video. So the Chinese women really did outperform Orlando in this event. Good for them. Great work. But there's one thing that makes the news report extremely misleading. The Chinese women's team finished 25th in that day's competition, and Orlando finished 38th. That's a respectable result for the Chinese women, especially considering that they outperformed plenty of other teams. But they weren't even the highest-ranking Chinese women's team that day. China Police Team E, another all-female team, finished 24th. And the best-performing women's team on day three actually came from Kazakhstan. It was a team called Tamiris, which finished 21st. Yes, Kazakhstan. I know, I was quite surprised too. And for those who don't know, Kazakhstan is actually my home country. So you go, girls. But now let's look at the men's results. The fastest team on day three was Kazakhstan A, which completed the challenge in just over two minutes. That's almost an entire minute faster than the Chinese women's team featured in the video. And remember how the news outlet presented this as Chinese women using superior technique to beat American men relying on brute strength? Well, China also had four men's teams participating in the tournament, and two of them finished fourth and sixth on day three, both significantly faster than the Chinese women's team featured in the video. In fact, China Police Team A completed the challenge in approximately 2 minutes and 18 seconds. That's 30 seconds faster than China Police Team F. So apparently Chinese men also know a thing or two about technique. But what if we look beyond day three? What happened in the overall competition across all five challenges? Well, this is where things get even more interesting. The overall winner was Kazakhstan Team C, which took gold with 536 points. Silver went to Kazakhstan Team A with 515 points, and bronze went to China Police Team C with 493 points. All three were men's teams. And yes, I was just as surprised to find out that Kazakhstan had such strong SWAT teams. Apparently, we won both gold and silver in an international competition involving 109 teams. Hey, you live, you learn. Now, what about the women? Well, the highest-ranking all-female team was once again Kazakhstan Tamiris. They finished 18th overall out of 109 participating teams, which, if you think about it, is a very impressive achievement. They finished ahead of 91 other teams, most of which were all-male teams, and they were the only all-female team in the top 20. The Chinese women's team F, featured in the viral video, finished 28th overall, which is also a very respectable result. And for those who are interested, Orlando Police Department finished 43rd. So yes, the Chinese women beat Orlando. They also outperformed many other men's teams throughout the tournament. But sorry ladies, there were also plenty of men's teams that performed better than them. In fact, the first 17 places in the overall competition were taken by all-male teams. Which brings me back to news.com.au. They could have made a perfectly legitimate story about a Chinese women's SWAT team performing very well in an international competition. They could have highlighted the fact that these women outperformed numerous men's teams. They could even have celebrated their technique and teamwork. And all of that would have been perfectly fine. But instead, they selected one Chinese women's team and one American men's team, showed footage of their separate runs side-by-side, and presented it as if they were racing head-to-head. They left out the actual rankings and the broader results of the competition, giving viewers a very misleading impression of what actually happened. And that's what frustrates me about this kind of reporting. You have a genuinely impressive achievement by a women's tactical team, something absolutely worth celebrating. And if you look at the full results, you find even more impressive performances, including the women's team from Kazakhstan, which finished higher than the Chinese team featured in the video. But instead of giving viewers the full picture, they turned it into another men vs women story. And the thing is, you don't have to manipulate the presentation to make these women look good. Their actual results are impressive enough. And maybe, just maybe, a major news outlet should be more interested in showing its audience what actually happened than in finding another excuse to fuel the gender war.
